analysis.title: 'Are We There Yet?' Morgan Stanley Maps The Rotational Bear Market Breaking Europe Under The Surface
key_insights: MS European equity strategy (Marina Zavolock and team) says rotations under the STOXX 600 surface are at bear-market proportions across six trades: high vs low momentum, AI capex plays vs the 'debated disrupted', Strait of Hormuz closure vs reopening, cyclicals vs defensives, bond proxies and the highly levered, and French sovereign risk. The index itself is only c. 3% off its all-time high.

European 12x1M price momentum (top quintile vs bottom) has drawn down 14% from its June highs, 12% of it in October. Top momentum stocks fell 7% relative from June highs to recent lows while bottom momentum rose 9%, which MS reads as a single trade unwinding.

The current momentum episode is 4.1 months old, with top vs bottom down 16%. That is slightly worse than 2011 and 2021 (-13%) and a fraction of the dot-com unwinds (-27% to -35%). Besides 2006, it is the only comparable episode where cyclicals also fell sharply (-12%). MS notes comparable unwinds have preceded both index breakdowns and melt-ups.

MS's 'fundamental momentum' measure (earnings and price-target revisions plus idiosyncratic momentum) is down 13% from its summer highs. MS says unwinds there tend to be tactical and short-lived, so recoveries are more consistent than in plain price momentum.

The ratio of European core AI enablers (semis, part of cap goods and tech hardware) to 'AI challenged' names (software, business services, media, medtech) is down 38% from its June peak (-42% at the lows) and fell 23% in October alone (-29% at the lows). At the trough it had erased 52% of its gains since November 2022 and nearly two-thirds of its YTD relative gains.
AI 'losers' recovered nearly 90% of their YTD relative losses at the peak of the rebound.

European cyclicals (including banks, excluding defence) are down 13% relative to defensives, comparable to or slightly worse than recent growth scares: -10% in the 'AI disruption dominoes' and start of the Iran war, -12% around Liberation Day, -11% in the summer 2024 'Sahm Rule' episode. Excluding AI-challenged names, the cyclical hit deepens to 15%. MS says cyclicals vs defensives has completed 'a full growth scare cycle'.
Defensive squeeze: Medtech, Life Sciences, Pharma and Tobacco are up 14% from recent lows, and Food & Beverage, Food Retail and HPC are up 8%.

MS flags a squeeze in bond proxies as yields came off highs, which 'appears to be at the top of a tactical range'. A small rally in Europe's most levered stocks is 'likely to be short-lived, even if bond yields continue to decline somewhat'.

MS's Strait of Hormuz sensitivity screen shows the ratio of stocks hurt by a closure vs those helped has fallen back to its April lows. MS links oil and the war, together with US 10Y yields breaking 5%, to a growth scare that hit everything from OAT spreads to the AI complex. Yields are now back below 5% 'for now'.

If a deal to reopen the Strait comes, MS's sensitivity work says Airlines, Aerospace, Discretionary Retail and Luxury gain the most, with the DAX and mid-caps the most exposed indices. The article notes deal headlines are moving the wrong way: WSJ reported the US told Gulf states to prepare for a short, intense campaign after the midterms, Qatar presented Iran a new draft deal that a senior Iranian official denied, and European natgas was near €100.

French stocks with the highest OAT-spread sensitivity and domestic exposure are near the relative lows of the June 2024 snap election. On a 52-week z-score basis they hit -3.9 standard deviations, the deepest on MS's chart since 2021 (-3.2 currently).

MS argues European corporates, including banks, have limited direct exposure to OAT spread widening, and that the French rotation was mostly about global financial conditions via rising bond yields. With yields off highs, pressure 'eases some' as French equities come off 'highly oversold levels'.

European banks (SX7E) had a 30-day drop MS says resembles the 2022 post-Russia/Ukraine pullback. Historically a 13-15% 30-day decline has been a trough signal, with an 89% hit rate one month out (+7.4% average) and 84% six months out (+19.8%). The article notes the 2022 analogue also included a Credit Suisse event seven months in.

The main French risk per MS is the tax bill, not the bond spread. Proposals include LFI's higher corporate tax surcharge (MS estimates ~8.8% of CAC 2027 earnings and 135bp of MSCI Europe's), a revenue-profit 'mismatch' tax, a 33% buyback tax, and RN's tax on 'excess' dividends that could cut CAC 2027 dividend yield from 3.3% to 2.3%. Clarity is 'unlikely until mid-next year at the earliest'.

MS built a rebound score combining price momentum, fundamental momentum, AI enabler vs challenged exposure, Hormuz sensitivity and cyclical vs defensive positioning. Semis, Tech Hardware, Cap Goods, Metals & Mining and Banks would lead a rebound, while defensives from Medtech and Tobacco to Food & Bev are most at risk. By country, the Netherlands, Austria and Ireland would lead, with Denmark, Belgium and Norway lagging.

Top of MS's buy-the-reversal stock screen: Nokia, VAT Group, Nebius, Infineon, STMicro and ASM International, then Boliden, Siemens Energy, Atlas Copco and ACS. Banks fill much of the back half (BPER, ABN Amro, Raiffeisen, Santander, ING, UniCredit). Most at risk if the rotation reverses: Lindt, EssilorLuxottica, Philips, Smith & Nephew and Centrica, plus telcos, tobacco and pharma including Novo Nordisk and AstraZeneca.

MS broadly sees an attractive risk-reward for a rotational rebound. The ZeroHedge author is skeptical: all the rebound signals depend on unresolved issues (who funds AI capex, whether oil and gas keep bonds on edge, whether Paris passes a budget that spares corporate earnings), and the market has priced the growth scare but probably not the next one.

trade_ideas.description: Long the European rotational rebound basket: semis, tech hardware, cap goods, metals & mining and banks, including Nokia, VAT Group, Nebius, Infineon, STMicro, ASM International, Boliden, Siemens Energy, Atlas Copco, ACS, and banks BPER, ABN Amro, Raiffeisen, Santander, ING, UniCredit

trade_ideas.risk: Unresolved funding of AI capex, oil and gas keeping bond markets on edge, and French budget and tax outcomes. Comparable momentum unwinds have preceded both breakdowns and melt-ups.

trade_ideas.risk: A further growth scare would extend the defensive bid.

risk_factors: Unresolved funding of the AI capex build-out.
Oil and gas prices keeping the bond market on edge, with US 10Y yields having broken 5%.
French budget and tax proposals (LFI surcharge, buyback tax, RN excess-dividend tax) with clarity unlikely before mid-next year.
Hormuz deal headlines moving against reopening, including a possible US military campaign after the midterms and European gas near €100.
Historical unwinds like the current one have preceded both index breakdowns and melt-ups.
The 2022 bank-pullback analogue also included a Credit Suisse event about seven months in.

vol_and_positioning: European 12x1M momentum (top vs bottom quintile) has a 14% drawdown from June highs, 12% in October. Top and bottom legs mirror each other (-7% and +9% relative), which MS reads as a single positioning purge.
MS says bear-market-level rotations under the index surface have greatly challenged consensus positioning.
The momentum unwind is 4.1 months old with top vs bottom down 16%, versus 2011 and 2021 (-13%) and the dot-com unwinds (-27% to -35%).
Defensives squeezed: Medtech, Life Sciences, Pharma and Tobacco +14% and Food & Beverage, Food Retail and HPC +8% from recent lows.
Bond proxies show a squeeze that MS says appears to be at the top of a tactical range. The rally in Europe's most levered stocks is likely short-lived.
French stocks with the highest OAT-spread sensitivity and domestic exposure hit -3.9 standard deviations on a 52-week z-score, the deepest reading since 2021.
geopolitical: Strait of Hormuz closure and the Iran war: MS's Hormuz sensitivity ratio is back at April lows, the level of lowest investor sentiment on the conflict.
WSJ reported the US told several Gulf states to prepare for a short, intense military campaign after the midterms.
Reuters reported Qatar presented Iran with a new draft deal, which a senior Iranian official denied.

French fiscal and budget uncertainty: Moody's review of France took place last Friday, and the OAT-Bund spread hit EU crisis-level highs earlier this month. France has no budget and tax proposals from LFI and RN are on the table, with clarity unlikely until mid-next year at the earliest.
cross_bank_references: Goldman's Bobby Molavi called the past few weeks 'unplayable' on Monday (cited by the article, US context).
Morgan Stanley's Nick Savone argued on Sunday that the glass is half full for US equities.
Morgan Stanley colleagues first laid out how to survive 'The Great Momentum Unwind' (Aug 3).

tension_points.bull_case: MS sees an attractive risk-reward for a rotational rebound: cyclicals vs defensives has completed a full growth scare cycle, Hormuz-sensitive stocks are at April lows, bond proxies are stretched, French stocks are near -3.9 standard deviations and banks flash a historical trough signal with an 89% one-month hit rate.
tension_points.bear_case: The article argues all rebound signals rest on the same unresolved issues (AI capex funding, oil and gas pressure on bonds, a French budget that spares corporate earnings). Hormuz deal headlines are moving the wrong way and European gas is near €100, so the market may have priced this growth scare but not the next one. Comparable unwinds have preceded both breakdowns and melt-ups.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A further US 10Y yield spike back above 5%, a French budget with large corporate tax increases, or Hormuz escalation, such as the reported US military campaign after the midterms.
